steps.label: Six families of tools · 1/10
steps.speakerNotes: KP03 defined the task of outputting a class but not the algorithm. This unit compares the assumptions of classifiers.

steps.label: Six families of tools · 1/10 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: The first three: Bayes-type methods model each class's density, logistic regression models class probability directly, KNN compares neighbors.

steps.label: Six families of tools · 1/10 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: The other three: trees split space step by step, SVMs find a margin boundary, ensembles combine models. The lines are conceptual groups, not historical lineage.

steps.label: Six families of tools · 1/10 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: These families overlap, and none is best on every dataset.

steps.label: Prior, density, posterior · 2/10
steps.speakerNotes: For continuous X and finite classes: the posterior is the prior times the density, divided by the sum over all classes.

steps.label: Prior, density, posterior · 2/10 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: The prior pi j: the class share before seeing the features.

steps.label: Prior, density, posterior · 2/10 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: The class-conditional density f j: how concentrated the class is near a position. A density can exceed 1.

steps.label: Prior, density, posterior · 2/10 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: The posterior: class probability after seeing the features. For a continuous distribution P(X=x) is 0; writing a density as P(X=x) mixes up point probability and density. With correct posteriors and equal costs, picking the maximum has the smallest expected error, though not every case is right.

steps.label: Densities at x = 0.7 · 3/10
steps.speakerNotes: The source's example: apple is class 1, cucumber class 2, one roundness measurement x. Means 0.8 and 0.2, both standard deviations 0.1, priors 0.5 each. The vertical axis is density, not point probability.

steps.label: Densities at x = 0.7 · 3/10 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: At roundness 0.7: near the apple mean, far from the cucumber mean.

steps.label: Densities at x = 0.7 · 3/10 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: The apple's standardized distance is minus 1, the cucumber's is 5. With the common factor 3.989422804, the apple density is about 2.4197 and the cucumber's about 0.0000149.

steps.label: Densities at x = 0.7 · 3/10 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: The source's guide lists about 0.24 and 0.0001 and posteriors 0.9996 and 0.0004 for the same parameters, which disagree with the Gaussian formula; we keep the parameters and recompute.

steps.label: The posterior · 4/10
steps.speakerNotes: Multiply by the prior: apple q1 is 0.5 times 2.4197, about 1.2099; cucumber q2 about 0.0000074.

steps.label: The posterior · 4/10 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: The sum is the evidence density, about 1.2099.

steps.label: The posterior · 4/10 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Normalize: the apple posterior is about 0.999994 and the cucumber about 0.000006, summing to 1. When comparing classes you may drop the common denominator but not different priors.

steps.label: The posterior · 4/10 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: All values were recomputed by program and checked digit by digit against the note.

steps.label: A tie · 5/10
steps.speakerNotes: The interactive component has another default: means 3 and 7, standard deviation 1, priors 0.5 each, x equal to 5.

steps.label: A tie · 5/10 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: At x equal to 5, both classes are 2 away from their means.

steps.label: A tie · 5/10 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: So both densities equal 0.053990967, each weighted density is 0.026995483, the evidence is 0.053990967, and each posterior is 0.5. It is a tie; outputting one class still needs a tie rule.

steps.label: A tie · 5/10 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: These values were also recomputed by program.

steps.label: LDA and QDA · 6/10
steps.speakerNotes: A supplement: fix the two class means (−1, 0) and (1, 0) and equal priors, and vary only the covariance. The dots mark means, not training samples.

steps.label: LDA and QDA · 6/10 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: LDA lets both classes share the covariance diag(1, 0.5): the quadratic terms cancel and the equal-posterior boundary is the straight line x1 equal to 0.

steps.label: LDA and QDA · 6/10 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: QDA gives each class its own covariance, here diag(0.4, 0.8) and diag(1.8, 0.3). The boundary becomes curved. It is solved from equal log-scores, with no data fitted.

steps.label: LDA and QDA · 6/10 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: FDA is a criterion for choosing a projection direction; under a two-class shared-covariance Gaussian model its direction corresponds to LDA's, but they are not identical procedures in every setting.

steps.label: Logistic regression · 7/10
steps.speakerNotes: Logistic regression skips the class densities and models the binary posterior with a sigmoid. The basic form is binary; multi-class is an extension.

steps.label: Logistic regression · 7/10 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: The output is a probability between 0 and 1. This curve is a sketch with b equal to 0 and beta equal to 1, not a training result.

steps.label: Logistic regression · 7/10 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: The point where the probability is 0.5 is the boundary.

steps.label: Logistic regression · 7/10 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: The basic form has linear log-odds in the binary case.

steps.label: KNN and decision trees · 8/10
steps.speakerNotes: These sketches are not the note's data. KNN finds the k nearest neighbors by distance and votes on their labels.

steps.label: KNN and decision trees · 8/10 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: The star is the point to classify; the circle holds its 3 nearest neighbors and the majority decides. Not fitting parameters does not mean no assumptions: distance, feature scaling and k all matter.

steps.label: KNN and decision trees · 8/10 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: A decision tree splits the space level by level with feature thresholds. A single tree is sensitive to data changes, and depth controls complexity.

steps.label: KNN and decision trees · 8/10 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: CART, ID3 and C4.5 are historical names within the decision-tree family.

steps.label: SVM and ensembles · 9/10
steps.speakerNotes: An SVM trades margin against errors. The solid line is the boundary, dashed lines the margin edges, circled points the support vectors. This is the hard-margin, separable simplification; soft-margin support vectors can lie inside the margin or even be misclassified, so only caring about points nearest the boundary needs a condition.

steps.label: SVM and ensembles · 9/10 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Kernels use inner products in an implicit feature space without computing high-dimensional coordinates, but a suitable kernel is needed; they guarantee neither separability nor universally better accuracy.

steps.label: SVM and ensembles · 9/10 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Ensemble methods combine models. Random forests often grow many trees by resampling and feature randomization then aggregate; boosting fixes earlier shortfalls in turn. They differ.

steps.label: SVM and ensembles · 9/10 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Trees and ensembles are overlapping concepts.

steps.label: Rule of thumb · 10/10
steps.speakerNotes: Rule of thumb: ask how scores are produced, then which assumptions the data can challenge.

steps.label: Rule of thumb · 10/10 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Each family produces scores differently and has its own checkable assumptions.

steps.label: Rule of thumb · 10/10 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Misconception: a hard-to-estimate class density does not mean Bayes cannot be computed; toy examples can be computed directly, and high-dimensional estimation is the practical problem.

steps.label: Rule of thumb · 10/10 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: The note's 4 self-check questions stay in the note. The next unit turns to numerical prediction and dimensionality reduction.
